title: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections)
hook: if God needs nothing, why make a world at all? the Brahma Sutra's answer is one word: play
tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaishnava theology, freedom was brass polished back to its own shine: a self still itself, sharing every joy except running the world. What good thing in you showed again? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.
screen: `THE SHINE COMES BACK.` · `TODAY: WHY MAKE A WORLD?`

segments.voice: A child's question, and a philosopher's too: if God already has everything, why make anything? People act because they lack something. We cook because we're hungry, work because the rent is due, build because the roof leaks. A being who lacks nothing has no reason to lift a finger. So either God needed the world, which would mean God wasn't complete, or the world has no reason at all. The Brahma Sutra raises this objection itself, plainly, as a problem for anyone who says Brahman made the world. Then it answers in a handful of words. On our last day with the Sri Bhashya, we hear how Ramanuja unpacks them.
screen: `IF GOD HAS EVERYTHING, WHY MAKE ANYTHING?` → `WE ACT BECAUSE WE LACK.` → `THE SUTRA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The sutra's answer: it is only lila, play, as in the world. Ramanuja gives the picture. A great king who already rules everything, who wants for nothing, still plays a game with a ball, just for the joy of it. Nobody says he's playing because he's short of something. The play comes out of fullness, not need. So too, he says, the Lord brings forth the world, holds it up and draws it back, as play. Not because he lacks, but because he's full. Notice what this does. For Ramanuja the world is real, and it's held close: the world and every self are like the Lord's body, as yesterday's lesson put it. So this play isn't a trick or a dream. It's real, it's close, and it rests in someone who is joy itself. Now look back across this week with him. A book that states the other view first. Without qualities read as without bad ones. Knowing as a thread of oil that becomes love. A lamp and its light. A self freed into its own shine. And today, a world made from fullness, as play. That's Vaishnava theology in a few strokes: careful argument, all of it in service of a God the Alvars sang to. Tomorrow the same Brahma Sutras open again, read through another great commentator, Shankara, with jnana, knowing, at the center.
screen: `ONLY PLAY, AS IN THE WORLD.` · `A KING WHO PLAYS BALL.` · `FROM FULLNESS, NOT NEED.` · `A REAL WORLD, HELD CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in what's already full. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice how much of today has run on lack: something to fix, something to get, something to finish. Let that be there. Then, for a few breaths, notice what's already enough right now: the breath arriving on its own, the floor holding you, light in the room. Let the breath move as if it were play, not work. If you pray, you can rest in the name you pray to, and in the world held close. The bell holds the time.
Vaishnava theology. Today, lila: a world made not from need but from fullness, as play, real and held close by the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: Vaishnava theology (Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, selections). Today, do one small thing for no reason but joy, the way a king plays ball. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas speak of creation as the Lord's lila, his play, and celebrate it in festivals and stories of Vishnu's descents; students meet the argument in the Sri Bhashya's comment on the Brahma Sutra's second chapter.

fork.setup: someone objects: a God who needs nothing has no reason to make a world. you're Ramanuja. how do you answer?
options: then God must have needed the world after all.
then the world can't really exist.
it's play, like a king with everything who still plays a game.
fork.reveal: following the Brahma Sutra, Ramanuja says creation is lila: play that comes from fullness, not need.

original.note: Sanskrit: play, the Brahma Sutra's word for why the Lord brings forth the world.

trapdoor: what you thought: if the world is God's play, it isn't serious.
what it means: for Ramanuja, play means the world comes from God's fullness, not his need, and it's fully real.
what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 2.1.32–33, 'lokavat tu lila kaivalyam', with the Sri Bhashya's image of a king at a ball game.
